You'd probably have to determine a formula for "a few bucks" since this is going to be where you gain or lose users.

Let's say you go with a fixed price af $3. That doesn't sound bad when you're buying a $400 TV, but it sounds like a LOT when you're buying a $5 lamp. So, you're going to have to use some sort of sliding scale based on the product.

But which scale do you use? Do you base it on the price of the product or on the price of the projected savings? If you base it on the price of the product, you will get people who like going to auctions suggesting items that aren't actually great deals, since the higher price will fetch them a higher return. So, in order to curb this, you'll have to use the projected savings as a basis for what these "finders" make... The higher the projected savings, the more they make, enticing them to suggest the best deals in an attempt to make the most money.

Now you have to find a way to compare the auction price with what the current "value" actually is... And that can be a HUGE undertaking, depending on how big your user base is.

If you have the for it, you could probably make this successful... Hell, an app that compares gas station prices was successful... You just have to put in the time, effort, and research.
Or you could have it request based, i.e. I'd pay $2 for a good bargain on a coffee table, any takers?

Probably wouldn't use it myself, but it sounds like a great idea. Your main hurdle won't be developing it though, it'll be convincing enough people to use it to make it worthwhile. Oh, and a tonne of financial regulation stuff if you're going to be acting as an escrow agent.
